title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: "Some time passed before I learned my friends' full history. It was a story that couldn't fail to make a deep impression on me, since it revealed a number of circumstances, each one interesting and wonderful to someone as utterly inexperienced as I was.

"The old man's name was De Lacey. He came from a good family in France, where he'd lived for many years in comfort, respected by those above him and loved by his peers. His son had served his country, and Agatha had ranked among the highest ladies of society. A few months before I arrived, they'd lived in a large, luxurious city called Paris, surrounded by friends and possessing every advantage that virtue, a refined intellect, or taste, together with a moderate fortune, could provide.

"Safie's father had caused their ruin. He was a Turkish merchant who had lived in Paris for many years. For some reason I couldn't learn, he'd fallen out with the government. He was arrested and thrown into prison on the very day Safie arrived from Constantinople to join him. He was tried and sentenced to death. The injustice of this sentence was outrageous. All Paris was furious. It was widely believed that his religion and wealth, rather than the crime he was charged with, had been the real cause of his condemnation.

"Felix happened to be present at the trial. His horror and outrage were uncontrollable when he heard the verdict. He immediately swore a solemn vow to free the prisoner, then looked for ways to do it. After many failed attempts to get into the prison, he found a heavily barred window in an unguarded part of the building. It opened into the dungeon of the unfortunate Muslim, who waited in chains for his barbarous execution. Felix visited this window at night and told the prisoner his plans. The Turk, amazed and delighted, tried to secure Felix's loyalty with promises of reward and wealth. Felix rejected these with contempt. But when he saw beautiful Safie, who was allowed to visit her father and whose gestures expressed her deep gratitude, the young man couldn't help recognizing that this captive possessed a treasure that would fully reward his effort and risk.

"The Turk quickly saw the impression his daughter had made on Felix. He tried to bind Felix more firmly to his cause by promising Safie's hand in marriage once they reached safety. Felix was too honorable to accept this outright. But he looked forward to it as the fulfillment of his happiness.

"During the preparations for the escape, several letters from the lovely girl further warmed Felix's devotion. She'd found a way to express her thoughts in her lover's language with the help of an old servant of her father's who knew French. She thanked Felix in the most passionate terms for his efforts to help her father. At the same time, she gently mourned her own fate.

"I have copies of these letters. I found writing materials during my time in the hovel, and the letters were often in Felix's or Agatha's hands. I'll give them to you before I leave. They'll prove the truth of my story. But since the sun is already low, I'll only have time to summarize their contents.

"Safie told how her mother was a Christian Arab who had been captured and enslaved by the Turks. Her beauty won the heart of Safie's father, who married her. The young girl spoke with pride and passion about her mother, who had been born free and rejected the bondage she was now subjected to. She taught her daughter the principles of her Christian faith and instilled in her a desire for intellectual independence and freedom of spirit — things forbidden to Muslim women. When this lady died, her lessons remained indelibly imprinted on Safie's mind. Safie was sickened by the prospect of returning to Asia, where she'd be confined to a harem and allowed only childish amusements ill-suited to her character, which had grown accustomed to grand ideas and noble ambitions. The prospect of marrying a Christian and staying in a country where women held a place in society enchanted her.

"The day of the Turk's execution was set, but on the night before it he escaped from prison. By morning he was many leagues from Paris. Felix had obtained passports in his own name, his father's, and his sister's. He had already told his father the plan. The old man left his house under the pretense of a trip and hid with his daughter in a remote part of Paris.
"Felix led the fugitives through France to Lyons, across Mont Cenis, a pass over the Alps, to Leghorn, where the merchant planned to wait for a chance to reach Turkish territory.

"Safie decided to stay with her father until he left. Meanwhile the Turk renewed his promise that she would marry her rescuer. Felix stayed with them, enjoying the company of the Arabian, who showed him the simplest and most tender affection. They talked through an interpreter, and sometimes communicated with looks alone. Safie sang to him the divine music of her homeland.

"The Turk allowed this closeness and encouraged the young lovers' hopes — while secretly planning something quite different. He despised the idea of his daughter marrying a Christian but feared Felix's anger if he seemed reluctant, knowing Felix still had the power to betray him to the Italian authorities. He devised a thousand schemes to keep up the deception until it was no longer necessary, planning to secretly take his daughter with him when he left. His plans were helped by news from Paris.

"The French government was enraged by the prisoner's escape and spared no effort to find and punish his rescuer. Felix's role was quickly discovered. De Lacey and Agatha were thrown into prison. The news reached Felix and shattered his happiness. His blind, aging father and gentle sister were in a foul dungeon while he enjoyed freedom and the company of his beloved. This thought was torture. He quickly arranged with the Turk that if the latter found a chance to escape before Felix could return to Italy, Safie would stay at a convent in Leghorn. Then, leaving his beloved Arabian, he rushed to Paris and surrendered himself to the law, hoping to free his father and sister.
"He failed. They were imprisoned for five months before the trial, which stripped them of their fortune and condemned them to permanent exile from France.

"They found a miserable refuge in the cottage in Germany where I discovered them. Felix soon learned that the treacherous Turk — the man for whom he and his family had endured such unimaginable suffering — had turned traitor upon discovering his rescuer was ruined. He'd left Italy with his daughter, insultingly sending Felix a small sum of money to help him, as the Turk put it, with some plan for supporting himself in the future.

"These were the events that weighed on Felix's heart and made him, when I first saw him, the most miserable of the family. He could have endured poverty. When it was the price of virtue, he gloried in it. But the Turk's ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were misfortunes more bitter and irreparable. The Arabian's arrival now breathed new life into his soul.

"When the news reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his wealth and position, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return home. Safie's generous spirit was outraged by this command. She tried to argue with her father, but he stormed off, repeating his tyrannical order.

"A few days later, the Turk burst into his daughter's room and told her urgently that he had reason to believe his hiding place in Leghorn had been revealed and that he would soon be handed over to the French government. He'd hired a ship to take him to Constantinople and would sail within hours. He planned to leave his daughter in the care of a trusted servant; she would follow at her leisure with most of his property, which hadn't yet reached Leghorn.

"Left alone, Safie considered what to do. A life in Turkey was unbearable to her. Both her religion and her feelings were against it. Through some of her father's papers that fell into her hands, she learned of her lover's exile and the name of the place where he now lived. She wavered for a time, but finally made her decision. Taking some jewels and a sum of money, she left Italy with an attendant — a woman from Leghorn who spoke Turkish — and headed for Germany.

"She arrived safely at a town about twenty leagues from the De Lacey cottage, where her attendant fell dangerously ill. Safie nursed her with the utmost devotion, but the poor woman died. The Arabian was left alone, unable to speak the local language and completely ignorant of how the world worked. But she fell into good hands. The Italian woman had mentioned their destination before she died, and the woman of the house where they'd been staying made sure Safie reached her lover's cottage safely."
